definition: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, causing the temperature of the surroundings to increase. Examples include combustion, neutralisation, and respiration.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, causing the temperature of the surroundings to decrease. Examples include thermal decomposition and dissolving ammonium nitrate.
The minimum amount of energy required for a reaction to start. Reactant particles must collide with at least this much energy for bonds to break and a reaction to occur.
The energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond, measured in kJ/mol. Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic); forming bonds releases energy (exothermic).
The process of breaking chemical bonds in reactants. This is always endothermic — it requires energy input.
The process of forming chemical bonds in products. This is always exothermic — it releases energy.
A diagram showing how energy changes during a chemical reaction. Shows the energy of reactants, products, activation energy, and whether the overall reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
Another name for an energy profile diagram. Shows the energy of reactants and products and the activation energy barrier that must be overcome.
The difference between the energy absorbed to break bonds and the energy released when new bonds form. If more energy is released than absorbed, the reaction is exothermic.
In exothermic reactions, the temperature of the surroundings increases. In endothermic reactions, the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
A device that produces electricity through an electrochemical reaction between a fuel (usually hydrogen) and oxygen, without combustion. Produces water as the only product.
A type of fuel cell that uses hydrogen as the fuel. Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to produce water and generate electricity. It is a clean energy source with no carbon emissions.
An exothermic reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen to produce energy. Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.
An exothermic reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water. The temperature of the surroundings increases.
An endothermic reaction in which a substance is broken down into simpler substances by heating. Energy must be continuously supplied.
An experimental method used to measure the heat energy transferred in a chemical reaction, by measuring temperature changes in a known mass of water.
The amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. For water, this is 4200 J/kg°C.
